# Education, Social Sciences, & Sports Graphs {#sec-graphs-education-social-sports}

The graphs in this chapter are available from the `r keys("Education")`, `r keys("Social Sciences")`, and `r keys("Sports")` buttons in the **Graphs** section of the **Analyses** tab.
Along with the options described here, each graph's editor includes the [shared pages](#sec-editor-common) (e.g., **Axes**, **Legend**, and **Placement**).

## Scale Chart {#sec-scale-chart-dlg}

*Education*

A scale chart places scores along one or more labeled scales (e.g., letter grades or proficiency levels), so that each score can be read against them.
The dataset should have one row per score, with an ID to label the point and (optionally) the group that it belongs to.

::: {.tipsection data-latex=""}
The dataset's ID column provides the label for each point, so fill it with meaningful names.
:::

### Variables {-}

**Score**: The value to place along the scales (e.g., a test score).

**Grouping** (optional): Splits the scores into groups (e.g., by student), with each group's scores shown separately.
A blank group is placed into a *[NO GROUP]* category.

### Options {-}

**Scale values**: Enter the values shown along the scales' axis.

**Precision**: Enter the number of decimal places shown for the scale values.

**Scale header**: Enter the header shown above the scales.

**Data header**: Enter the header shown above the scores.

**Showcase score**: Check this option to make most of the graph translucent, except for the areas of the scales where the scores fall.
This draws attention to the parts of the scales that have scores in them.

### Scales {-}

The **Scales** page defines the scales that the scores are read against (e.g., the ranges of letter grades).
Use the `r keys("Add")` and `r keys("Remove")` buttons to change the list of scales.

Each scale has a **Header** and a list of **Blocks**.
Each block has the following:

- **Label**: The block's label (e.g., *F (fail)*).
- **Length**: How much of the scale the block covers.
- **Color**: The block's color.

\newpage

## W-Curve Plot {#sec-wcurve-dlg}

*Social Sciences*

A W-curve plot shows how each observation's measurement changes over a series of time intervals (e.g., students' sense of belonging across semesters or years).
The dataset should have one row per observation per time interval, holding the measurement, the interval, and the observation's name.

### Variables {-}

**Y (sentiment)**: The measurement being tracked (e.g., a sense of belonging or a satisfaction score).

**X (time interval)**: The period that the measurement was taken in (e.g., the semester or year).
Values should start at 1 and usually go up to 4, although up to 12 is supported.

**Grouping**: The name or ID of each observation (e.g., a student).
Each one is drawn as its own line.

### Options {-}

**Time interval label**: Enter the label for the time intervals (e.g., *semester* or *year*).

### Showcasing {-}

**Ghost opacity**: Enter the opacity of the lines that are not showcased.

**Showcase lines**: Add the observations to highlight, while the others are shown faded.

## Linear Regression Roadmap {#sec-lr-roadmap-dlg}

*Social Sciences*

A linear regression roadmap shows the results of a linear regression as a road leading to a goal.
Predictors that help are placed along the way, and those that hinder are shown as obstacles.
The dataset should have one row per predictor from the regression, with its name, coefficient, and (optionally) p-value.

### Variables {-}

**Predictor**: The name of each independent variable from the regression.

**Coefficient**: The coefficient of each predictor.
Positive values are drawn as positive influencers and negative values as negative ones.

**p-value** (optional): The p-value of each predictor.
Predictors with a p-value above the **p-value threshold** are left off the road.

### Options {-}

**Dependent variable description**: Enter a description of the dependent variable (i.e., the goal at the end of the road).

**Show predictors**: Select which predictors to show (**All**, **Positive only**, or **Negative only**).

**Marker labels**: Select how each predictor is labeled (**Name only**, **Name and value**, or **Name and absolute value**).

**p-value threshold**: Enter the highest p-value that a predictor can have to be included.

**Road color**, **Lane separator**, **Road stop theme**, and **Add explanatory caption**: These are the same as the [**Pro & Con Roadmap**](#sec-procon-roadmap-dlg) options.

\newpage

## Win/Loss Sparkline {#sec-win-loss-sparkline-dlg}

*Sports*

A win/loss sparkline shows the outcome of every game in a season as a compact row of marks, with home games, shutouts, and streaks easy to spot.
The dataset should have one row per game, with the season it belongs to and codes for its outcome, whether it was a shutout, and whether it was a home game.

### Variables {-}

**Season**: The label of the row that each game is placed in (e.g., the season or team).

**Won/Lost**: The outcome of each game (won, lost, or tied).
A blank cell marks a game that was canceled or a scrimmage.
It is skipped when finding streaks and other statistics.

**Shutout**: Whether the game was a shutout.

**Home game**: Whether the game was played at home.

**Postseason** (optional): Whether the game was a postseason game.

::: {.notesection data-latex=""}
Games are placed in the order that they appear in the dataset.
:::

### Options {-}

**Highlight best records**: Check this option to highlight the best season record(s) and the longest winning streak(s).
These are determined across all the seasons.
